title: Beautiful on the inside: Aesthetic preferences and the skeletal complexity of shapes

findings.mechanism: The 'Goldilocks' effect suggests an optimal level of complexity for aesthetic appeal, where moderately complex shapes are 'just right'.
findings.quote: participants chose moderately complex shapes (54.6%) significantly more frequently than both simple shapes (43.8%; t(192) = 4.97, p = 1.45 × 10-6, d = .36)

findings.mechanism: The 'Goldilocks' effect suggests an optimal level of complexity for aesthetic appeal, where moderately complex shapes are 'just right'.
findings.quote: and overly complex shapes (42.5%; t(192) = 4.09, p = 6.32 × 10-5, d = .29)

findings.mechanism: A quadratic relationship indicates an inverted-U pattern, where preference peaks at an intermediate complexity level.
findings.quote: a significant quadratic term for the relationship between complexity level and chosen probability (b = -1.75, 95%CI[−2.21, -1.29], t = −7.47, p < 2.59 × 10-12)

findings.mechanism: Overall variation in aesthetic preference is driven by the manipulated complexity levels.
findings.quote: a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant effect of complexity level (F(4,768) = 10.12, p = 1.68 × 10-4, η² = 0.054)

findings.mechanism: The 'Goldilocks' effect is stronger when the underlying skeletal structure (higher-level complexity) is preserved, suggesting it's not just low-level features.
findings.quote: moderately complex stimuli were chosen much more often in the Intact group than in the Scrambled group, (with the difference in moderate vs non-moderate being 11.4% for the Intact group vs. 2.9% for the Scrambled group, t(498) = 5.18, p = 3.24 × 10-7, d = .46).

findings.mechanism: Overall variation in aesthetic preference is driven by the manipulated complexity levels across both intact and scrambled conditions.

findings.mechanism: Confirms the robust inverted-U 'Goldilocks' effect for intact shapes, where aesthetic preference peaks at moderate complexity.

findings.antecedent: complexity level (quadratic term) for scrambled shapes
findings.mechanism: A subtle 'Goldilocks' effect persists even when skeletal structure is destroyed, suggesting some influence of low-level visual features on aesthetic preference.

stimuli.description: Algorithmically generated 2D polygons, manipulated for skeletal complexity (5 levels from simple to complex) within 30 'families'. Rendered as abstract brush drawings on framed canvases in a virtual room.
Box-scrambled versions of the 2D polygons from Experiment 1, created by dividing each image into a 6x6 grid of 90px x 90px boxes and randomizing their positions.

limitations: The stimuli were mounted on a fixed background (a gallery room), which might influence participants' choices. Future work could vary the context to explore its role in the relationship between complexity and beauty.
